summary:
Most prophetic books speak to a people on God's behalf; Habakkuk speaks to God. The book is a dialogue between the prophet and God, capped by a prayer. The first complaint is about Judah, where "the law is paralyzed" (1:4): "How long, O LORD, must I call for help but You do not hear" (1:2). God's reply names His instrument: "I am raising up the Chaldeans — that ruthless and impetuous nation" (1:6). The Chaldeans are the Babylonians, which places the book in the closing decades of the 600s BC, during Babylon's rise; it took Jerusalem in 586 BC. The second complaint objects to the remedy: "Why are You silent while the wicked swallow up those more righteous than themselves?" (1:13).

Habakkuk then waits: "I will stand at my guard post and station myself on the ramparts" (2:1). The answer is a vision to write plainly on tablets (2:2), its center a single line: "the righteous will live by faith" (2:4). The Hebrew behind "faith," emunah, also means faithfulness. The New Testament quotes this line three times: Romans 1:17, Galatians 3:11, and Hebrews 10:38. Five taunts against the conqueror follow, each beginning "Woe" (2:6, 9, 12, 15, 19), with a promise in their midst: "For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea" (2:14).

Chapter 3 is a prayer marked like a psalm: the heading "according to Shigionoth" is a musical term whose meaning is lost; "Selah," probably a musical pause, appears three times; and the last line of the book is a performance direction: "For the choirmaster. With stringed instruments." The prayer recalls God's past acts — plague going before Him, the sea trampled by His horses — and asks, "In Your wrath, remember mercy!" (3:2). Habakkuk trembles at what is coming (3:16), then resolves: "Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, though the olive crop fails and the fields produce no food, though the sheep are cut off from the fold and no cattle are in the stalls, yet I will exult in the LORD; I will rejoice in the God of my salvation!" (3:17–18).
